https://www.dw.com/en/indonesia-mount-br.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IVhH Strong winds and steep terrain have made it difficult for firefighters to contain the blaze Image: East Java Regional Disaster Mitigation Agency/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement Authorities in Indonesia closed the Bromo Tengger Semeru National Park in East Java until further notice on Saturday due to a wildfire that has scorched some 176 hectares (435 acres) of land on Mount Bromo since it began on Monday. The blaze, one of several currently burning across Indonesia, has mobilized hundreds of firefighters, park rangers, police, soldiers and volunteers at one of Indonesia's most popular tourist destinations. What do we know about the wildfires situation in Indonesia? Helicopters and drones are in use in the air and firebreaks are being created by crews on the ground. Officials describe the situation as challenging, pointing to high winds and rough terrain, with many areas difficult to access on steep volcanic slopes. "These conditions make air operations important to reach areas that cannot be accessed optimally by land," one official said. The blaze has mobilized hundreds of firefighters, park rangers, police, soldiers and volunteers at one of Indonesia's most popular tourist destinations Image: Muhammad Fajri/Anadolu Agency/IMAGO Dry conditions and winds are fueling the spread of the flames according to Indonesia's Meteorological, Climatological and Geophysical Agency. Authorities say the fire was sparked during land clearing work. Though fires — often illegally started by plantation owners and farmers to clear for planting — are common in the region, the current El Nino weather pattern and seasonal dry winds from Australia have combined to make this year especially prone to wildfire and drought . Indonesia has lost more than 107,000 hectares of land to fire in the first half of 2026, over twice the area destroyed in wildfires in 2023, when the last El-Nino pattern started. Drone strikes hit key Ukraine-Poland supply route, sparking border fires Copy/paste the link below: Copy Copy/paste the article video embed link below: Copy Updated: 14/09/2026 - 9:27 GMT+2 Ukraine said a Russian drone strike ignited a fire at a petrol station near the Yahodyn–Dorohusk border crossing with Poland in the early hours of Sunday, 13 September. Video filmed close to the crossing showed flames and thick smoke as firefighters tackled the blaze. … More Falling drone debris set fire to a petrol station and several trucks near the Yahodyn border crossing in western Ukraine, according to Valentyna Chernysh, a spokesperson for the Volyn Customs Service. She told Ukrainian public broadcaster Suspilne that the checkpoint itself was not hit and remained intact. No one was injured. ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT Border operations were temporarily suspended during the air-raid alert as customs staff and travellers took shelter. Processing later resumed as emergency workers dealt with the damage. Footage from the scene showed firefighters and other emergency personnel at the petrol station, as well as damage to a nearby road. The incident came as Russian drones targeted several areas in western Ukraine, which has so far been largely spared the heaviest fighting seen in the east. The overnight strikes also hit a Kyiv-Warsaw passenger train near the border, damaging its locomotive about two kilometres from Poland, according to Ukraine’s state railway operator Ukrzaliznytsia. No one was injured after passengers and crew were evacuated following an advance warning. The Yahodyn-Dorohusk crossing is one of the main road routes for military and humanitarian supplies entering Ukraine from Poland and other Western allies. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the strikes near the border were more than an attack on Ukraine’s frontier, describing them as “Putin’s terror ‘knocking’ directly on the doors of the EU and NATO” and calling on European countries to tighten sanctions against Moscow. Polish officials said the strike site was about 800 metres from the Polish border and confirmed that no injuries had been reported on the Polish side. Ukrainian and Polish authorities were continuing to assess the impact of the attacks. https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: The City of Sydney has banned smartglasses in all its pools, libraries, gyms, childcare centres and town halls. The council agreed to update signage and guidance to prevent people wearing the glasses in community facilities, due to growing privacy and harassment concerns. In a statement, Greens councillor Matthew Thompson said his motion included exemptions for those who use the glasses as accessibility devices, including those with vision and hearing loss. He urged the federal government to do more to regulate the glasses and prevent their misuse, saying that: Overseas we’re seeing women being targeted and harassed in public and recorded without their consent. We don’t want what’s happening in the US to happen here. That’s why we’re banning smart glasses and other wearable recording devices from all of our pools, gyms, childcare [centres], libraries and other council spaces. Cheap wearable devices like smart glasses are already flooding the market. But instead of stopping this problem

Photograph: Connie Chornuk/Disney/Getty Images Music Choosin’ Texas unseats All I Want for Christmas as longest-running No 1 song on Billboard Hot 100 Ella Langley’s record-breaking song has spent 23 weeks at the top, surpassing Mariah Carey’s holiday anthem Maya Yang Tue 22 Sep 2026 15.45 EDT Last modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 15.57 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Ella Langley’s hit song Choosin’ Texas has made Billboard Hot 100 history, spending 23 weeks on the chart and breaking the record for the longest-running No 1 song in the chart’s 68-year old history. The track, which was released last October as the lead single on the 27-year-old singer and songwriter’s album Dandelion, has surpassed Mariah Carey’s All I Want for Christmas Is You, which topped the charts for 22 weeks. ‘It sounds good next to almost anything’: how Choosin’ Texas became the biggest song of the year Read more Choosin’ Texas first appeared on the Billboard Hot 100 last November. Co-written by Miranda Lambert, Luke Dick and Joybeth Taylor, the heartbreak track’s success has been described by Langley as “surreal”. “I think this has been the biggest moment for me, where I’ve seen where fans can change your career. For so long, you’re like, ‘Alright, one song at a time, one record at a time.’ But with this one song – and they’ve done it continuously for me – but really with ‘Choosin’ Texas’ … man, have they taken ahold of it. It’s wild,” Langley told Billboard in an interview earlier this year. The song follows a Tennessee-based narrator watching her partner leave for another woman in Texas, transforming a familiar story of heartbreak into one that occurs not only between three people but between two places. “Just when I thought I got him to fall in love with Tennessee / I shoulda known better than to take him back to Abilene / I put him right back into her arms / I wasn’t a match for that kind of spark,” Langley sings in the opening verse. “She’s from Texas, I can tell by the way / He’s two-steppin’ ‘round the room / And judgin’ by the smile that’s written on his face / There’s nothin’ I can do.” Other country references in the song include “Smoky Mountain rain,” “Memphis blues,” and Tennessee’s famous Jack Daniel’s whiskey. Describing its origins, Langley told Billboard: “I was on a writers retreat with Miranda, our first time writing together. At a young age, she had a pet kangaroo. She told me how she got pulled over once with the kangaroo in the passenger seat. The kangaroo got her out of a ticket and she said, ‘Of course, I had Texas plates, too.’ I went, ‘Well, she’s from Texas, I can tell … ’ Forty-five minutes later, we had the song written.” Victoria Banks, a Nashville-based songwriter instructor at Belmont University, pointed to the song’s simplicity and familiarity as a reason for its success. “Everything about the song throws back to a simpler time in country music that people are really craving,” Banks told the Guardian in July, adding: “All of these writers have been working in the Nashville market for years … So even though this is a song that they said they spat out in 30 minutes or whatever, it was coming through their instincts that have been developed for a long time about what is hooky and what pulls people in.” Explore more on these topics Music Mariah Carey Country news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed Film Books Music Art & design TV & radio Stage Classical Games Design a better world

https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/13/rent.text: Rental prices in Georgia and Armenia rose 20–30% year on year over the summer as Russians fearing a new wave of mobilisation for Russia's ongoing war in Ukraine sought accommodation in former Soviet republics where they can stay without a visa.Georgia remains the most accessible destination: Russian citizens can stay for up to 360 days without a visa and reset the clock with a brief visit to a neighbouring country. Tens of thousands now live there.In Tbilisi, monthly rents for standard housing start at €450–730, rising to €910–2,700 or more for larger flats or upmarket apartments. The average nominal monthly wage in Georgia stands at around 2,165 lari, or roughly €750, according to the National Statistics Office.After a summer peak, rents in Georgia have fallen and broadly stabilised. The sharpest increases came in 2022–2023, when rents jumped 60–70% following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022.Russians accounted for more than 55% of all property transactions involving foreign buyers in 2023, but their share has since fallen by a third.In 2026, Georgians made up 76% of transactions in Tbilisi's primary housing market, according to investment bank Galt & Taggart, with Israeli buyers at 11% and Russians at 3%. Demand is more diversified in the Black Sea city of Batumi.Russians driving up Armenia’s rental marketDemand is most acute in Armenia, where Russians — and Armenians who had been living in Russia and are seeking to avoid mobilisation — are concentrating mainly in Yerevan.Monthly rent for a two-room flat in the capital currently runs to €800–900. Russian citizens can enter without a visa and stay for up to 180 days per year.A 10% tax now required when registering lease contracts with the Cadastre is typically passed on to tenants.According to Armenia's Cadastre Committee, average prices for flats in Yerevan apartment blocks rose 2.9% in August from July and were up 23.5% on a year earlier. Russian nationals account for around 72% of all property transactions carried out by foreign nationals in Armenia.In August, foreign citizens took part in 506 purchase and sale transactions nationwide, representing 7.6% of all deals, with 70.2% of those purchases — 177 properties — made in Yerevan.The average nominal monthly wage in Armenia is 320,763 dram (€790), with substantially higher pay in sectors such as IT, finance and mining.Belarus nextBelarus has drawn Russians since Moscow's all-out war began, first as a transit point and later as a place to stay.After partial mobilisation was announced in September 2022, demand for short- and medium-term rentals in Minsk and border cities such as Brest and Gomel surged sharply.With European borders closed to Russians and sanctions tightening, Belarus has since attracted longer-term residents and property buyers.Russian citizens can remain without registration for up to 90 days, while a long-term rental contract qualifies them for a temporary residence permit. Unlike Russia, Belarus has not imposed sweeping internet restrictions.Russian buyers now account for more than 10% of all property transactions in Belarus, up from 2% a year ago, according to the National Cadastral Agency.Demand among Russians for residential property in Minsk rose 10–15% in 2026, and the city's housing price per square metre increased 25.6% over the year.The two largest waves of emigration from Russia since the full-scale invasion came in 2022: first in February and March, then in September, when President Vladimir Putin announced partial mobilisation.

https://www.digi24.ro/stiri/externe/rusi.text: Vladimir Putin a propus o misiune umanitară comună ruso-ucraineană în orașul Kosteantînivka, din estul Ucrainei, unde, potrivit liderului de la Kremlin, ar mai fi între 400 și 500 de civili. Propunerea a fost transmisă reprezentanților americani aflați la Moscova. În același timp, președintele rus a reafirmat că Rusia nu va accepta desfășurarea trupelor occidentale în Ucraina după încheierea războiului, avertizând că acestea ar fi considerate „ținte legitime”, potrivit France24 . Putin a sugerat că operațiunea ar putea urma modelul unei inițiative similare desfășurate în octombrie, care le-a permis locuitorilor din orașul Oleșkî, aflat sub control rusesc, să părăsească zona. Potrivit liderului de la Kremlin, operațiunea din Oleșkî a inclus și livrarea de ajutoare umanitare pentru persoanele care au ales să rămână în oraș. Putin a mai declarat că Rusiei i-au trebuit cinci zile pentru a demina zona din apropierea orașului Kosteantînivka, relatează Interfax. Liderul rus a afirmat că între 400 și 500 de civili se mai află în Kosteantînivka și a sugerat că o operațiune comună cu Ucraina ar putea facilita evacuarea acestora și furnizarea de ajutoare umanitare. Propunerea vine în contextul luptelor intense din estul Ucrainei, unde Kosteantînivka reprezintă un punct important pentru apărarea ucraineană în regiunea Donețk. În discuțiile cu reprezentanții americani, Vladimir Putin a reiterat și opoziția Moscovei față de desfășurarea unor trupe occidentale pe teritoriul Ucrainei, ca parte a unui eventual acord de pace sau a unor garanții de securitate pentru Kiev. Prezența militarilor străini în Ucraina reprezintă una dintre cerințele importante susținute de Kiev în negocierile privind o eventuală încetare a focului și menținerea păcii după încheierea războiului. Putin a avertizat că Moscova ar considera orice trupe străine desfășurate în Ucraina drept „ținte legitime”. Mai mult, liderul rus a susținut că o asemenea desfășurare ar însemna, în realitate, „continuarea războiului”. Declarațiile evidențiază divergențele majore dintre poziția Moscovei și cea a Kievului în privința viitoarelor garanții de securitate pentru Ucraina, în condițiile în care desfășurarea unor forțe internaționale este discutată ca posibilă componentă a unui acord de pace.
